Prologue

The lamp had not been lit for eleven years when the first letter
arrived. It came in a plain brown envelope, addressed in a careful hand
to The Keeper, as though the post office had simply forgotten that there
was no longer any such person.

Nobody in the village could say who had carried it up the cliff path. By
morning it was lying on the step, weighted down with a smooth grey
stone.

Chapter One

Mara Ellison had inherited three things from her grandfather: a brass
telescope, a talent for silence, and the key to a building that the
council wanted demolished. She kept all three in the same drawer and
tried not to think about any of them.

“You could sell it,” her brother said, not for the first time. “The land
alone must be worth something.”

“It is not for sale, Tomas.”

“Everything is for sale. That is the whole point of money.”

She did not answer him. Outside the kitchen window the tide was coming
in, and the long shadow of the tower lay across the water like the hand
of a clock. She had watched that shadow every evening of her childhood
and she knew, without looking at her watch, that it was nearly seven.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

The letter was waiting when she climbed the path the next morning. She
turned it over twice before she opened it, and afterwards she wished
that she had left it where it lay.

Light the lamp on the ninth, it said. Someone is coming home.

There was no signature. There was only a small drawing in the corner of
the page, a ship with three masts, and she had seen that ship before,
carved into the underside of her grandfather’s desk.

Chapter Two

The harbour master was a broad, slow-moving woman named Agnes Thorne who
had never once been surprised by anything. She read the letter at arm’s
length, the way she read everything, and handed it back.

“Well,” she said. “That is your grandfather’s ship, right enough. The
Corriveau. Lost with all hands in the winter of sixty-one.”

“I know when it was lost.”

“Then you know nobody is coming home on it.” Agnes folded her hands.
“Somebody is having a joke with you, girl. An unkind one.”

Mara wanted to believe her. It would have been the sensible thing to
believe. But she had already counted the days, and the ninth was a
Thursday, and on Thursday there would be no moon at all.

She bought lamp oil on the way back up the hill. She told herself that
it was only because the price was good.

Chapter Three

By the ninth the whole village knew. They came up the path in ones and
twos as the light failed, pretending that they had only come to see the
view, and stood about on the wet grass with their collars turned up
against the wind.

Tomas came last, carrying a flask of tea and a blanket, and said nothing
at all, which was the kindest thing he had done in years.

At a quarter to nine Mara climbed the one hundred and forty-two steps,
trimmed the wick the way she had been taught as a child, and struck a
match.

The beam went out across the black water. For a long moment there was
nothing. Then, far out beyond the bar, a second light answered.
